tips.tip: Add 'po' or 'opo' to show respect to elders: 'Salamat po', 'Opo'.
Tagalog often puts the verb first: 'Kumain ako' literally means 'Ate I'.
'Ng' marks the object (Gusto ko ng tubig) while 'ang' marks the topic of the sentence.
'Apo' is a respectful way to address an elder or someone of high status.
'Unay' intensifies: 'Agyamanak unay' means 'Thank you very much'.
'Pu' is the Kapampangan politeness marker, like Tagalog 'po'.
'Ing' works like the Tagalog 'ang' to mark the topic: 'Nanu ing lagyu mu?'
'Dios mabalos' (May God repay you) is the usual way to say thank you.
'Nin' marks the object, like Tagalog 'ng': 'Gusto ko nin tubig'.
Cebuano uses 'og' before an indefinite object: 'Gusto ko og tubig'.
'Dili' negates future or habitual actions; 'wala' negates past actions.
Hiligaynon uses 'sang' before an indefinite object: 'Gusto ko sang tubig'.
'Gid' adds emphasis: 'Madamo gid nga salamat' is a heartfelt thank you.
Waray uses 'hi' before personal names: 'Ako hi Juan'.
'Hin' marks an indefinite object: 'Karuyag ko hin tubig'.
Mindanao Bisaya often borrows Tagalog words, e.g. 'pangalan' instead of Cebuano 'ngalan'.
'Kaayo' means 'very': 'Salamat kaayo' means 'Thank you very much'.
'Magsukul' comes from the Arabic 'shukr', meaning gratitude.
Tausug greetings often follow Islamic custom: 'Assalamu alaikum'.
Chavacano words come mostly from Spanish, but the grammar is Philippine: 'Quiere yo agua' puts the verb first.
'Ya' marks a completed action: 'Ya come ya tu?' means 'Have you eaten?'.

culture_items.title: Pahiyas Festival
culture_items.description: Held every May in Lucban, Quezon, to thank San Isidro Labrador for a good harvest. Houses are decorated with colorful kiping (rice wafers).

culture_items.title: Barong Tagalog
culture_items.description: The embroidered formal shirt of Filipino men, often woven from piña (pineapple) fiber.

culture_items.title: Intramuros
culture_items.description: The old walled city of Manila, built during Spanish rule. Its stone walls, gates and Fort Santiago still stand along the Pasig River.

culture_items.title: Vigan
culture_items.description: A Spanish colonial town in Ilocos Sur with cobblestone streets and ancestral houses, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

culture_items.title: Pinakbet
culture_items.description: An Ilocano vegetable dish of squash, eggplant, ampalaya and okra, flavored with bagoong.

culture_items.title: Vigan Empanada
culture_items.description: A crispy orange rice-flour pastry from Ilocos Sur, filled with egg, green papaya and Vigan longganisa.

culture_items.title: Dagupan Bangus
culture_items.description: Dagupan City in Pangasinan is famous for its bangus (milkfish) and holds a yearly Bangus Festival.

culture_items.title: Sisig
culture_items.description: A sizzling dish of chopped pork seasoned with calamansi and chili. It comes from Pampanga, the culinary capital of the Philippines.

culture_items.title: Giant Lantern Festival
culture_items.description: Held in San Fernando, Pampanga every December. Huge parol (star lanterns) with thousands of lights flash in time with music.

culture_items.title: Bicol Express
culture_items.description: A spicy Bicolano dish of pork cooked in coconut milk with plenty of chili.

culture_items.title: Pancit Batil Patung
culture_items.description: A noodle dish from Tuguegarao, Cagayan, topped with a poached egg, meat and vegetables and served with egg-drop soup.

culture_items.title: Sagada Hanging Coffins
culture_items.description: In Sagada, Mountain Province, the Kankanaey (Applai) people traditionally placed the coffins of their dead on cliff sides.

culture_items.title: Ivatan Stone Houses
culture_items.description: Thick-walled houses of limestone and coral with cogon roofs, built in Batanes to withstand strong typhoons.

culture_items.title: Vakul
culture_items.description: A headgear made from vuyavuy palm fiber, worn by Ivatan women in Batanes to protect them from the sun and rain.

culture_items.title: Hudhud Chants
culture_items.description: Long narrative chants of the Ifugao, sung during rice harvesting, funerals and weddings. UNESCO lists them as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

culture_items.title: Batok
culture_items.description: Traditional hand-tapped tattooing of the Kalinga, made with a thorn and soot. Apo Whang-Od of Buscalan is its best-known mambabatok.

culture_items.title: Sinulog
culture_items.description: Cebu's grand January festival honoring the Santo Niño, with dancers moving to the rhythm of drums.

culture_items.title: Lechon
culture_items.description: Whole roasted pig. Cebu's version is famous for its crisp skin and herb-stuffed meat.

culture_items.title: Dinagyang
culture_items.description: Iloilo City's festival featuring energetic warrior-dance performances.

culture_items.title: La Paz Batchoy
culture_items.description: A rich noodle soup from Iloilo topped with pork, crushed chicharon and garlic.

culture_items.title: Pintados Festival
culture_items.description: Held in Tacloban, Leyte. Dancers are painted to look like the tattooed warriors the Spanish called 'pintados'.

culture_items.title: Ati-Atihan
culture_items.description: A festival in Kalibo, Aklan, where participants paint their faces and dance in the streets.

culture_items.title: Piña Cloth
culture_items.description: A fine, sheer fabric woven in Aklan from pineapple-leaf fibers, often used for the barong Tagalog.

culture_items.title: Binirayan Festival
culture_items.description: A festival in San Jose de Buenavista, Antique, recalling the legendary arrival of ten Bornean datus on Panay.

culture_items.title: Capiz Shell Windows
culture_items.description: Window panes and lamps made from thin, translucent capiz (windowpane oyster) shells, a craft linked to Capiz province.

culture_items.title: Rodeo Masbateño
culture_items.description: A rodeo festival in Masbate, a province of cattle ranches, with lassoing and bull-riding contests.

culture_items.title: Romblon Marble
culture_items.description: Romblon is known for its high-quality marble, carved by local artisans into sculptures, tiles and furniture.

culture_items.title: Cuyo Fort
culture_items.description: A Spanish-era stone fortress around a church in Cuyo, Palawan, built to protect the town from raids.

culture_items.title: Kinilaw
culture_items.description: Fresh raw fish 'cooked' in vinegar or citrus with ginger, onion and chili, a favorite in coastal Visayan towns such as those of the Camotes Islands.

culture_items.title: Kadayawan
culture_items.description: Davao City's thanksgiving festival celebrating the harvest and its indigenous cultures.

culture_items.title: Durian
culture_items.description: Davao is famous for durian, a spiky fruit with a strong smell and a sweet, creamy taste.

culture_items.title: Pangalay
culture_items.description: A graceful Tausug dance from Sulu, often performed with long metal fingernail extensions called janggay.

culture_items.title: Pastil
culture_items.description: Steamed rice topped with shredded chicken or beef, wrapped in banana leaf. A Maguindanaon favorite.

culture_items.title: Kulintang
culture_items.description: A row of small bronze gongs played with drums and larger gongs. The Maguindanaon are known for their kulintang music.

culture_items.title: Okir
culture_items.description: Flowing, curving designs carved in wood and brass by the Maranao and other Mindanao peoples.

culture_items.title: Torogan
culture_items.description: The large ancestral house of a Maranao sultan or datu, decorated with carved okir panels and a flared panolong.

culture_items.title: Singkil
culture_items.description: A Maranao dance in which a dancer steps gracefully between clapping bamboo poles, often while waving fans.

culture_items.title: Kaamulan Festival
culture_items.description: Held in Malaybalay, Bukidnon, it celebrates the cultures of Bukidnon's indigenous groups, including the Higaonon.

culture_items.title: Bonok-Bonok Festival
culture_items.description: Surigao City's yearly festival in honor of its patron, San Nicolas de Tolentino, with street dancing inspired by the region's indigenous rituals.

culture_items.title: Buklog
culture_items.description: A Subanen thanksgiving ritual held on a tall bamboo platform. UNESCO lists it as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

culture_items.title: Mabal Tabih
culture_items.description: The Blaan art of ikat weaving abaca cloth. Weaver Yabing Masalon Dulo received the National Living Treasures award for it.

culture_items.title: Fort Pilar
culture_items.description: A Spanish-era fort in Zamboanga City, now a shrine and a branch of the National Museum.

culture_items.title: Curacha
culture_items.description: A deep-sea spanner crab that is a specialty of Zamboanga City, often cooked in a rich coconut sauce.

culture_items.title: Yakan Weaving
culture_items.description: The Yakan of Basilan weave brightly colored cloth with bold geometric patterns on backstrap looms.

culture_items.title: T'nalak
culture_items.description: A sacred abaca cloth woven by T'boli women, whose patterns are said to come to them in dreams.

culture_items.title: Malong
culture_items.description: A tube-shaped woven cloth worn as a skirt, blanket, or hammock across Mindanao.

stories.title: The Legend of Daragang Magayon
stories.body: Long ago in Bicol lived Daragang Magayon, a maiden whose name means 'beautiful lady'. She fell in love with Panganoron, a brave chieftain's son, but a jealous suitor named Pagtuga waged war to take her. In the battle both lovers were lost, and they were buried together. From their grave rose a mountain of perfect beauty: Mayon Volcano. Its clouds are said to be Panganoron embracing his beloved, and its eruptions the anger of Pagtuga.

stories.title: The Legend of the Chocolate Hills
stories.body: One telling from Bohol says that two giants once quarreled across the land. For days they hurled rocks and sand at each other until they grew tired, made peace, and left the island together. They never cleaned up after their battle, and the scattered mounds became the Chocolate Hills. The legend reminds Boholanos that even a great quarrel can end in friendship.

stories.title: The Darangen
stories.body: The Darangen is the epic of the Maranao people of Lake Lanao. Sung over several days, it tells of the hero Bantugan and the kingdom of Bembaran, of courage, love, and the customs that bind a community. In 2005 UNESCO recognized the Darangen as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

stories.title: The Pearl of the Orient
stories.body: With the Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao Cores restored, their light joins together over the seas. Thirty voices become one song, many languages, one people. You have unlocked the Pearl of the Orient, a symbol of Filipino unity, identity and heritage. Keep speaking, keep listening, and keep these languages alive.
